before: A space between selectors can reach descendants at any depth. The > sign narrows the relationship to a direct child: an element immediately inside the selected parent.

In .shelf > p, .shelf selects the parent and p selects its direct paragraph children. The + sign selects the immediately following sibling with the same parent; ~ allows any following matching sibling. These signs describe relationships, not text characters to search for.

Keep all paragraphs navy except direct shelf paragraphs teal and every paragraph following the shelf purple. The supplied HTML stays in index.html; edit the CSS. The checks inspect this small page, not every possible browser or accessibility requirement.
after: A parent is an HTML part that holds other parts. A child is a part directly inside it. A descendant is anywhere inside it, even inside another child. The space in `.shelf p` chooses every paragraph inside the shelf.

For this project, start with navy paragraphs. Make the shelf’s direct paragraph children teal and its later paragraph siblings purple. If a new `div` wraps a shelf paragraph, that paragraph is no longer a direct child. The `>` rule will stop choosing it.

before.question: If a new div wraps Near note inside the shelf, will .shelf > p still select that paragraph?
choices: No; it is now a deeper descendant, not a direct child.
Only if its text is unchanged.
before.explanation: The new wrapper changes the parent relationship. A descendant selector could still reach the paragraph, but the direct-child selector cannot.

after.question: A new div wraps a paragraph inside the shelf. Does .shelf > p still choose that paragraph?
choices: No. It is no longer a direct child of the shelf.
Yes. The > sign means anything inside.
Only if its text stays the same.
after.explanation: The paragraph’s parent is now the div. A space selector can still reach it, but the direct-child selector cannot.
